title: I have a sister
goal: Express possession without a verb "to have", use the preposition *ag* that swallows its pronoun, and talk about family.
bekal: know the seven forms of *ag*: agam, agat, aige, aici, againn, agaibh, acu
name family members and ask about other people's families

notes: **Irish has no verb "to have".** None at all. Instead it uses *tá* plus the preposition *ag* ("at"): *Tá teach agam* — literally "there is a house at me". Compare the old English "the book is with me", or French *ce livre est à moi*: possession is something that sits *at* you.

**Ag swallows its pronoun into one word.** *Ag* + *mé* is never written separately; they fuse into *agam*. And so on: *agat, aige, aici, againn, agaibh, acu*. These are called prepositional pronouns, and Irish has a dozen prepositions that behave this way. The three most important — *ag*, *ar*, *le* — you'll master over the next three units.

**Tá Gaeilge agam — even a skill is a possession.** "I speak Irish" comes out as "there's Irish at me". The same pattern works for knowledge: *Tá a fhios agam* ("I know", literally "its knowledge is at me"), and for time: *Níl am agam* ("I don't have time").

**Níl agam ach deirfiúr amháin — "there isn't … but".** Irish has no word for "only". It uses a negative sentence plus *ach* ("but, except"): *Níl agam ach euro amháin* = "I have only one euro" — like English "I have but one euro". Note where *ach* goes: right before the thing being limited, not at the start of the sentence.

sections.title: Ag — the preposition that swallows pronouns

blocks.text: Watch the two forms that sound far from what you'd guess: *aige* is said "EH-guh" (not "AH-guh") and *aici* is said "EH-kih". Both come up constantly, so it's worth practicing them on their own.

blocks.title: Word-order traps
items: The thing owned comes **before** *agam*, not after it. *Tá carr agam*, not *Tá agam carr*.
When the owner is named, *ag* stands alone again: *Tá carr ag Seán*, *Tá Gaeilge ag mo dheirfiúr*. The fused forms are only for pronouns.

*Ag* also does a completely different job — marking an action in progress, as in *ag foghlaim* and *ag teacht*, which you've already seen. The two jobs are unrelated; the word after it tells you which is which.

head: Question
Say it
English
rows: Cé mhéad duine atá sa teaghlach?
How many people are in your family?

blocks.title: Clann isn't "clan"
items: *Clann* means **someone's children**, not a large kinship group. *Tá clann mhór aici* = "she has a lot of children".
The English word *clan* was indeed borrowed from it, but the meaning drifted a long way. For a clan or lineage, Irish uses *muintir* or *fine*.
*Muintir* also means "the people of": *muintir na hÉireann* = "the Irish people", *muintir Bhudi* = "Budi's family".

blocks.text: Since *ag* covers everything English says with "have", "can speak" and "know", it's one of the structures you'll use most often.

*Tá a fhios agam* is said "taw is AH-gum" — the *f* in *fhios* is completely silent, as you learned in the pronunciation chapter. It's one of the ten most-used sentences in Irish, so practice it until it comes out without thinking.

blocks.title: A subtle difference: agam and liom
items: *Tá sé liom* = "it's with me" (I'm carrying it, but it's not necessarily mine).
So if you borrow your neighbor's umbrella and someone asks where it is, the answer is *Tá sé liom* — not *Tá sé agam*, which would sound like you're claiming it.
